A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mCLM research despite the revised title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original oracle-model AUCs, predicted property changes for 430 FDA-approved drugs, and molecule-editing case studies.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds comparative drug-editing experiments, computational synthesizability evaluations, and molecular-block nearest-neighbor results.

M1.justification: V2 Algorithm 1 adds an explicit rule to select the property requiring the most improvement before proposing an edit; v1 enumerated functions without this priority rule. The tokenizers, GNN and adapter architecture, Qwen2.5-3B backbone, objectives, and training stages remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds a synthesis-compatible FDA-drug population and a synthesis-constrained editing scenario in Section 3.2. Coverage otherwise retains the same six ADMET endpoints, training sources, 430-drug study, and two failed-drug cases. This is a bounded extension within the existing drug-optimization domain.

E2.justification: V1 lacks competing molecule editors. V2 evaluates MoleculeSTM, FineMolTex, LDMol, GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Claude-3.5-Haiku against mCLM in Tables 1 and 3. It also compares MoleculeSTM and FineMolTex in retrosynthesis evaluation and adds MoleculeSTM to the retained fallen-angel experiment. The oracle-model comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new 122-drug evaluation restricts mCLM outputs to 582 synthesis-guaranteed blocks while allowing unrestricted baseline generation. V2 adds average relative improvement, SA scores, RDKit validity, and Allchemy-based synthesizability and makeability metrics. Allchemy testing selects the three best SA models and samples 200 generated molecules per model. Existing training budgets and oracle scaffold splits are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 extends the existing fallen-angel case study with MoleculeSTM, exposing invalid outputs during iterative editing. Appendix F.2 adds six block-neighborhood examples to examine representation quality. The original mCLM cases and frequent DILI modifications remain; no systematic component-ablation or sensitivity study is added.

E5.justification: V1 Table 1 reports p < 0.05 using a Wilcoxon test. The corresponding results in v2 Table 4 omit that statement, and the statistical-test references disappear. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars for the editing evaluations.

E6.justification: The original 430-drug property scores and all 24 oracle AUCs are retained. New results include 15.0% average improvement for mCLM versus 6.98% for Gemini-2.5-Flash on the 122-drug evaluation, and Table 2 makeability of 98.23% versus 85.39% for MoleculeSTM and 84.96% for FineMolTex. V2 also adds baseline case outcomes, neighborhood similarities, and a 12.87% aggregate for the retained 430-drug scores. The 122-drug results use different conditions from v1's main evaluation.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds an assembly-step derivation yielding 2n−3 reactions for n blocks, assuming the required blocks are available. V2 also defines makeability as validity multiplied by conditional synthesizability. The existing cross-entropy formulation changes only notation, and no substantial theorem or proof framework is introduced.

C1.justification: V2's abstract adds comparative claims about synthetic accessibility against seven generative methods, including GPT-5, and superior property performance on 122 synthesis-compatible medicines. These become central contributions alongside the retained bilingual modeling and iterative drug-repair claims.

C2.justification: V1 describes the fallen-angel proposals as suitable for automated assembly. V2 explicitly identifies those cases and the 430-drug experiment as lacking synthesis guarantees, and describes synthesis-compatible molecules as the intended application distribution. It also states the block-availability assumption for synthesis analysis and adds interpretations linking neighborhood similarity to representation quality and a DILI modification to Maji et al. (2023).

D1.justification: V2 documents Allchemy's 30-minute allowance per molecule, absence of substrate price limits, and metric definitions. It adds neighborhood-analysis details and explanations of dataset-table categories. Core implementation and training hyperparameters are retained, and code, data, and model release remain promised upon publication.

R1.justification: Section 4 shifts from separate chemical-modeling, functional-group, and general multimodal/multilingual surveys toward protein-language-model inspiration and direct positioning against molecule editors. V2 adds substantial protein-model literature, the new evaluated editors, and synthesizability references, while removing many general vision, audio, and multilingual references.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 merges vocabulary and tokenization sections, reverses the library-design and case-study order, moves Algorithm 1 and the original main experiment into appendices, and introduces a reproducibility statement. These are substantial narrative and organizational changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figures 1–3 and reformats the retained molecular-editing illustrations. It adds comparative tables, a MoleculeSTM case figure, and six neighborhood figures. The original 430-drug table is transposed and relocated, other tables and figures move, and document typography and page layout change throughout.

improvement.justification: V1's central comparative and synthesizability advantages had little direct evaluation. V2 substantially strengthens their assessment through seven editing baselines, a synthesis-constrained experiment, and Allchemy route-search evidence, while clarifying where synthesis guarantees do not apply. Dropped Wilcoxon reporting and the disagreement between Table 2 and its prose about MoleculeSTM synthesizability weaken reporting precision, but the comparative evidence and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement. The evidence remains computational rather than laboratory validation.
